#2056. 6 duels won, 4 key passes – ‘Mad’ Liverpool beast enjoys ‘brilliant’ performance for his country

One Liverpool player has been praised for his ‘brilliant’ performance for his country on Tuesday night.

Hungary’s two UEFA Nations League matches over the past week have been overshadowed by the fallout from Dominik Szoboszlai admitting that he played through the pain barrier for his country, a decision which hasn’t gone down well among some on Merseyside.

His club and international teammate Milos Kerkez was also in action for Marco Rossi’s side at home to Northern Ireland last night, and the 23-year-old’s efforts didn’t go unnoticed among the media.

Hungarian football writer Bence Bocsak took to X shortly after the final whistle in Budapest, where the match finished in a 1-1 draw, to praise the Liverpool left-back’s performance.

He posted: ‘Milos Kerkez was brilliant for Hungary tonight. The Liverpool man created the most chances in the game (4) and won the most tackles (2). Also won 6/7 duels and made 10 passes into the final third – the most on the pitch.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

While there was frustration for Kerkez and Szoboszlai over the result, which saw the Magyars miss their shot at automatic promotion to League A and instead face a two-legged play-off next March, the Liverpool defender can be especially pleased with his own contribution on Tuesday.

The figures below from Sofascore – some of which were also cited by Bocsak – illustrate the combative and creative attributes that the 23-year-old showed for Hungary last night.

Kerkez has started the bulk of our Premier League matches so far this season, even if at times he can still be overly impetuous to the extent that, after an accidental collision with Florian Wirtz against Bournemouth in September, Jamie Carragher described him as ‘a bit mad’.

However, he should take heart from his strong outing for his country, and Liverpool will need him to be even more assured and influential when Manchester United come to Anfield on Sunday.

It’d be the perfect occasion for our number 6 to deliver a statement performance and show that he can mature into being an integral presence in Andoni Iraola’s project on Merseyside.

#2054. Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end

Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

It was a shame because in that cameo, Fernandes showed he has returned from the World Cup in excellent shape, the tempo of United’s play immediately lifting when he had the ball. It is wrong to make conclusions in the summer, but you are on safe ground to state he will be integral to their ambitions.

Croke Park is a stadium steeped in history and another chapter was penned here, as the capacity crowd made this the highest attended soccer match in Ireland with 82,000 coming through the gates: it is a magnificent venue, one that would be well capable of hosting a Champions League final.

Michael Carrick hopes in years to come that is the stage where his team will be but, right now, it is a case of learning to walk again before they can run and he more than anyone will know how far off that target is, not that it will stop him trying to get there.

The one thing that is obvious about the way United play under him is the first thought from everyone is to go forward quickly. Yes, this was only a friendly, but the ambition to be on the front foot and cause problems was evident from the start.

The team in red had much the better of the opening exchanges, with Diogo Dalot having the first shot that went over but, unlike on July 25, when Mayo beat Kerry here in Gaelic football’s All Ireland final, which went viral, nobody was cheering the sight of a ball clearing the bar.

It was like a home game for United and the majority got what they wanted in the 15th minute when a slick counter-attack ended with Bryan Mbuemo sliding a pass into Joshua Zikzee, who rifled past James Trafford with a first-time finish.

Devastating counterattack! 💥Manchester United break and Joshua Zirkzee is there to finish it off 🤩 pic.twitter.com/y6QHbZMi7n

Zirkzee is unlikely to be part of Carrick’s squad beyond the transfer window, with interest from clubs in Italy, and it would be disingenuous to suggest his career at Old Trafford has been successful, but his attitude was exemplary and he played as if he was desperate to change his manager’s mind.

There may have been an anticipation that United would stride clear, but this game was also about Leeds, whose summer has been encouraging and whose confidence from staying up last season has evidently enabled them to blossom.

You would be way off the mark if you include them in your conversations about which clubs are going to be relegated next May, and the sense they showed to stay with Daniel Farke has paid off. They have bought some good players, not least goalkeeper James Trafford and Harry Wilson.

Top stop from James Trafford! 🚫The Leeds United keeper has been busy in the first half... pic.twitter.com/VKmxNVKBsA

Trafford has done the right thing getting away from Manchester City and you could argue that he is already reaping the benefit of playing for a manager who wants him, as he made a fabulous save in the 23rd minute to thwart Mbuemo. It was all part of performance that led to him being named player of the match.

He was involved in the move that brought the Leeds equaliser, too, as his long clearance caused uncertainty and led to Tyler Fletcher being pickpocketed by Dan James and he nudged a pass into Brenden Aaronson, who kept his cool and danced into the area, ignoring Senne Lammens, to finish.

Leeds hit back with their first shot on target! 💥Brenden Aaronson with a cool finish 🥶 pic.twitter.com/5WsSZY41j6

It was an entertaining affair, mercifully lacking the bile that would usually bubble away when it is staged in England, and the longer the game advanced, the better Leeds looked. They finished the opening period strongly and came back after the restart, with 10 changes, in the same fettle.

Farke, whose team had shown their ability to score heavily when they pummelled Liverpool 4-2 in Chicago 10 days ago, would have taken plenty of encouragement, but the perfectionist in him would have cursed the opportunities that were squandered early in the second period.

The misses proved costly as the game meandered and the shoot-out went United’s way, after Wilson and James Justin failed from 12 yards, with Noussair Mazraoui thumping in the decisive kick. It really is never dull.

Manchester United Lammens (Mee 61); Dalot (Mazraoui 60), Yoro, Heaven (Armer 46), Amass (Shaw 60); Santos (Collyer 46), T Fletcher (Tielemans 61); Diallo (J Fletcher 60), Zirkzee (Cunha 60), Dorgu (Thompson 46); Mbuemo (Fernandes 60).Subs not used Heath, Honor, Lacey, Gabriel.

Decent enough watch for roughly half the game, settled on a shoot-out in which Alex Cairns got nowhere near any of Manchester United’s penalties. Doubt he will lose much sleep over it. Bruno Fernandes grinned broadly when he missed.

Bottom left. Manchester United win the Boyle Sports Cup.

Smacks it even higher into the top right.

And I think Amapdu’s signal means Leeds will go first.

The ref decides to call time as the stewards cannot catch the juvenile intruders.

Not sure what we can say about stadium safety here but the game has ended prematurely after five kids came on, all of whom got to Bruno Fernandes to take selfies. It was very funny but, equally, plenty on the Manchester United bench were far from happy. Penalties to follow.

Some sealion ball juggling from Mazraoui involving foot, thigh and head, gets him past Justin on the right  but Gnonto heads away his cross.

Two young Man Utd fans run on to the pitch to try to take selfies with Man utd players. They are joined by three more and now another.

Bruno Fernandes lets fly from 20 yards, cushioning a pass from Tielemans before hammering his shot into the crossbar with little backlift.

Gnonto breaks down the right, plays it infield to Wilson who runs at the heart of the Man Utd defence but smacks his shot into a defender.

Cresswell blocks Mazroui’s shot with his right elbow which was pinned to his side and the ball falls to Bruno Fernandes but Cresswell is there again to block the shot, this time with his legs. From the corner, Bruno Fernandes balloons a long shot over the bar.

Enormous frustration for the masses who have wanted a Bruno goal. He’s just “scored” - right on the moment when our friend the stadium announcer bellowed the match was a sell out but never provided the actual figure – but a linesman’s flag has stopped him in his tracks. You fancy he will have one more involvement before the game creeps towards a penalty shootout.

Bruno Fernandes shoots past Cairns with a left-foot shot from 16 yards, smacking it inside the left post but the flag had long been raised.

The ball pinballs out to Justin by the D from the corner and he hammers a shot that Mee saves with great agility by the right post.

Excellent pass from Okafor from the left ought to have put Calvert-Lewin through but Armer does brilliantly to hold him up. Gnonto makes a run down the side but Calvert-Lewin checks back to shoot into Armer and the ball deflects behind for a corner.

Mazraoui drives down the right and feeds it inside to Fletcher whose deflected cross falls kindly for Thompson but the young striker cannot control it and Leeds recover.

Jack Fletcher is playing on the right with Tielemans and Collyer as the central two. Bruno Fernandes and Matheus Cunha are playing centrally with Thompson on the left. Nothing much happening as Leeds keep their defensive shape while Manchester United probe away.

Understandably Manchester United look disjointed now. Leeds have had longer for their changes to settle.

Seven Manchester United changes: Mee, Tielmans, Shaw, Bruno Fernandes, Jack Fletcher, Matheus Cunha and Mazraoui incoming for Dalot, Lammens, Amass, Mbeumo, Diallo, Zirkzee and Tyler Fletcher.

Couple of threatening crosses from Gnonto from the right just elude Calvert-Lewin and Alfie Cresswell, son of Richard, brother of Charlie, follows up the second to shoot from the edge of the box. Lammens gathers comfortably.

Just the 10 half-time changes for Leeds and the worst thing about that was the fact it gave the stadium announcer, who hadn’t grasped that he didn’t need to shout into a loud speaker system, the opportunity to screech unchecked for close to two minutes, leaving everyone with tinnitus. Give the wrong man a microphone and chaos will ensue. Anyway, we are underway in the second period and the one change the majority of the stadium wants to be see is the introduction of Bruno Fernandes. His presence would help United regain some impetus.

Huge cheer as Bruno Fernandes, Luke Shaw et al start to warm up.

Pleasant summer watch between largely second string players. Mbeumo looks a class apart from the other attacking players. The ref blows directly on 45 minutes moments after Nmecha rab out of room to control Tanaka’s cross and booted it out for a Man Utd goal-kick.

Manchester United probe patiently for half a minute around the Leeds area but the pass supposed to play Mbeumo through is picked off by Bijol and he plays it out to James who hares off down the left for 50 yards, cuts in on his right after leaving Yoro in his vapour trail, and whacks a shot over the bar from 22 yards.

United’s start has been bright and confident and the system they playing is flipping between 4-4-2 and 4-2-3-1 and the first thought is always to go forward. The goal they have just scored is indicative of how they have started and it’s a positive for Joshua Zirkzee, who has spent much of his time at Old Trafford under a cloud, to have finished it with aplomb. Whether it will be enough to keep him at Old Trafford for the long run remains to be seen, particularly as interest from Italy persists, but what can’t be doubted is his attitude. He looks sharp.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the pre-season friendly between Manchester United and Leeds United at a sold-out Croke Park in Dublin. Last year Leeds played Milan in the Irish capital and drew a crowd of 52,000 but at the GAA citadel, as I think I’m contractually obliged to call it, there will be 83,000 present, a testament to the Premier League’s reach and these two clubs’ popularity in Ireland founded on the exploits of Billy Whelan, Noel Cantwell, Johnny Giles, Roy Keane, Gary Kelly et al. It’s the first club match ever held at the stadium.

It’s a fixture that always stirs the blood and whenever it comes around you can guarantee that there will be reams of stuff about the War of the Roses, clash in styles, Busby and Revie, Bobby and Jack, large swathes of which this author has been guilty of producing. I’ll spare you all that today because while it’s relevant to fans of both clubs, they know it backwards. And it’s a match that has come around a wee bit too frequently in pre-season recently, first in Perth, Western Australia, in 2019 when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s side beat Marcelo Bielsa’s 4-0, then in 2023 in Oslo when Erik ten Haag’s second or third string defeated Daniel Farke’s threadbare, just relegated squad 2-0 and last year in Stockholm, which ended in a 0-0 draw between two scratch sides.

This one comes round later in the pre-season schedule than those three so we can expect to see stronger XIs, at least for part of the game. Leeds’ pre-season has gone well: after a 3-2 defeat by Wrexham in Tampa, they have beaten Sunderland in New Jersey, Liverpool in Chicago and RB Leipzig at Elland Road. Manchester United also lost to Wrexham (in Helsinki) then beat Rosenborg in Trondheim, Atlético in Stockholm and drew one apiece with the European champions, PSG, in Gothenburg last time out.

While Leeds will have new signing James Trafford available and Noah Okafor, who scored twice in Leeds’ first league victory at Old Trafford for 45 years last April, in the squad for the first time after the World Cup, Manchester United have Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford back in training since the start of the week but it seems too soon for them to start but Youri Tielemans is pushing to make his first start.

#2053. “Planning approval secured” : Stadium twist could change West Ham’s ownership plans

West Ham United’s window of opportunity to acquire their rented home for next to nothing appears to be fading. With £20 million of losses each year, the ground is a massive white elephant with the main tenant paying next to nothing for it’s bullet proof lease.

Former vice Chair Karren Brady, say what you like about her,  did at least negotiate the deal of the century giving West Ham a rock solid indestructible tenancy for generations to come. As the club were relegated, so the rent diminished leaving the owners to pick up the tab for West Ham’s failure on the pitch: An estimated £2.5 million each year is added to the tax payer burden thanks to the clause existing to reduce costs when West Ham dropped out of the Premier League.

Opportunities existed this summer, so we were told,  for the club to negotiate to buy the stadium, with suggestions that it would take £50 million for the deal to be done.

In the apparent lack of any take up by West Ham’s shareholders, the stadium owners have sought to bump up the former Olympic venue’s value in the meantime, by seeking to increase revenues through obtaining permission from Newham Council for a wider array of entertainment. According to London.stadium.com that effort has paid dividends:

Meaning the revenue which can be generated from the Stadium will be significantly higher, theoretically at least increasing its value and likely heading off West Ham’s options of acquiring it for next to nothing. Possibly.

West Ham’s London Stadium at night: There’ll be more events, louder music and bigger attendances – still won’t make a profit though. Just saying.

However the huge maintenance costs and temporary nature of the upper part of the structure means that even with consent for more events, bigger attendances and louder music, London Stadium is never going to become a lucrative, marketable venue in it’s current configuration.

Someone is going to have to spend hundreds of millions of pounds on fixing it: Like a giant pass-the-parcel game with a huge ticking time bomb of debt at the core of the fancy wrapping, neither West Ham nor the owners want to be left holding the bill when the music stops.

The difference is, the status quo favours the club, not the Greater London Authority who, as it stands, will find it pretty near impossible to turn a profit even with new approvals granted and new events lined up. And as every year passes, the need to spend big, big money on maintenance grows greater. In this instance, West Ham’s board biding their time and kicking it into the long grass for a few years yet is probably the shrewdest course of action. From the football club’s perspective.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

Brady may have got a deal, but our old ground wasn’t costing anything… you can’t play additional games (women, youth) and more importantly all other revenue, catering, naming rights, match day revenue on beer etc goes out the club, so in the world of Revenue is king, we can’t get any. That’s down to Brady’s skills, we’ll never be able to compete with the likes of Spurs etc.. The ground isn’t ours, so will never be a good deal , it’s soulless. IMO.

Am at a bit of a loss why a lot more live shows won’t make a lot more money? And why on earth as things stand now would West Ham want to spend millions buying the stadium when they are currently renting it for peanuts and all the hassle is passed onto the stadium operators?

There isn’t a revenue stream in the world that would make buying the stadium worthwhile for the current tenants. A point missed / ignored by the Brady haters.

#2052. Karren Brady’s New Agency Raises £104m West Ham Question

Former West Ham United vice-chair Karren Brady has launched a new commercial agency alongside fellow former Hammers director Nathan Thompson, specialising in sponsorship, hospitality and commercial strategy. The business, craetively called Brady Thompson, aims to help organisations unlock what its founders describe as hundreds of millions of pounds in untapped commercial value.

According to City AM, the pair have reunited just seven months after departing West Ham, with Brady talking enthusiastically about the enormous commercial opportunities available in sport and entertainment.

I have to say, I find it absolutely incredible that Brady has any sort of influence or clout in a business focusing on sponsorship, hospitality and commercial strategy, considering the Baroness was vice-chair when West Ham recorded losses of £104.2m in their last published accounting period. And that’s before we get onto the rather awkward subject of the London Stadium.

West Ham’s accounts for the financial year ending May 2025 revealed a pre-tax loss of £104.2m, a remarkable turnaround from the previous year’s £57.2m profit.

Now, clearly, not every penny of that loss can be attributed to Karren Brady. Football finances are complicated, and player recruitment, wages, transfer dealings and league performance all have a significant impact.

But she was one of the most senior executives at the football club, and surely the financial performance of the business has to form part of any assessment of her commercial legacy.

Indeed, Claret & Hugh previously reported that Brady had even become directly involved in negotiating transfers during the January 2026 window.

I’ve questioned the timing of her departure before, particularly given the financial difficulties and footballing problems that were developing towards the end of her time at the club.

So forgive me if I’m not immediately convinced by the idea that the same leadership can now teach other organisations how to maximise their commercial potential.

But perhaps the biggest irony of all is the decision to launch an agency specialising in sponsorship when, after ten years at the London Stadium, West Ham and the stadium authorities collectively failed to secure a naming-rights partner for the former Olympic venue.

A Premier League football club, based in London, playing in a stadium with a capacity of more than 60,000, and after a decade nobody managed to get a naming-rights deal over the line.

That wasn’t solely Brady’s responsibility, of course. The London Legacy Development Corporation controlled the stadium’s commercial arrangements, and there were disagreements about the value of any potential deal.

In fact, Brady herself pressed the stadium authorities to pursue naming rights, and the London Assembly has documented correspondence in which she expressed West Ham’s willingness to help secure an agreement.

Nevertheless, the outcome remains the same.

As Claret & Hugh reported last year, the stadium operators were warning that a naming-rights agreement might not materialise until 2028 or beyond.

And in my previous article about the missing £4m sponsorship opportunity, I argued that the failure to secure a partner when the stadium first opened had allowed the London Stadium name to become so established that selling it now would be considerably more difficult.

That is hardly a ringing endorsement of the commercial arrangements surrounding West Ham’s move from Upton Park.

Brady told City AM that unlocking commercial opportunities required imagination, experience, relationships and the willingness to challenge convention.

Nathan Thompson, meanwhile, pointed to his experience negotiating commercial deals from different sides of the boardroom.

I’m sure both have considerable contacts within the business world, and there’s no doubt Brady has spent decades operating at decent levels of football administration.

But contacts and experience are one thing. Results are another.

Perhaps the venture will prove enormously successful. Perhaps they’ll secure the sort of sponsorship agreements that other sporting organisations have struggled to attract.

However, from a West Ham supporter’s perspective, it is difficult to look beyond the £104m loss, the club’s subsequent relegation and the decade-long failure to find a stadium naming-rights sponsor.

When somebody starts offering advice about how to unlock hundreds of millions of pounds in commercial value, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to ask why so much potential remained untapped at the football club they helped run for 16 years.

But hey, if all else fails the new company name of Brady Thompson does sound like excellent branding for a luxury soap should they wish to diversify.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

I remember walking toward stadium a few season when an ad for a skip hire company based in Ilford was displayed on the “largest wraparound screen” in Europe, which itself is still attached to a former Olympic stadium at the time hosting a match involving London-based club. That just about sums Brady up. Lots of talk, but ultimately unable to transform that talk into commercial revenues for the club, in the way that has happened at, say, Spurs. Globally-significant, easily-recognisable brand names were always out of Karren’s reach when she was with us but no doubt she knew where to turn if she ever needed to hire a skip. Hard to magine her new agency being inundated with offers.

I think that’s a tad unfair, haven’t I heard ‘deal of the century’ attributed to her!

Maybe she can approach West Ham to offer us the benefit of her wisdom

Lots of sarcasm intended. But imagine if that were actually to happen!

One has to wonder who will be their favourite client? Mr 40% per chance?

Published: 18/11/2026 | Duration: 55 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson

In Episode 18 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch reflecting back on the time of Covid and a pre-Newcastle United takeover era that featured Steve Bruce, Mike Ashley and Joe Willock. A strange time indeed to be a United fan.

You can play episode 18 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Newcastle United’s difficult 2020-21 season under Steve Bruce, Joe Willock’s remarkable loan spell and the build-up to the Saudi-backed takeover are the focus as Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson return for the final instalment of their international break specials.

The trio revisit football behind closed doors, compare the pre-takeover squad with today’s Newcastle United and look ahead to the return of Bruno Guimarães with Arsenal.

The 2020-21 campaign was a strange time to be a Newcastle supporter. With St James’ Park largely empty due to Covid restrictions, Mike Ashley still in charge and Steve Bruce overseeing some desperately uninspiring football, the connection between supporters and their club was arguably at its lowest point.

Simon takes us back through the season, from the arrival of Callum Wilson and Ryan Fraser to the struggles of a side relying heavily on Allan Saint-Maximin for attacking inspiration. Despite spending much of the campaign uncomfortably close to the relegation places, Newcastle eventually finished 12th, thanks in no small part to Joe Willock’s extraordinary impact after joining on loan from Arsenal.

There’s also a moving personal story from Simon about his family’s experiences during lockdown, providing a reminder that football was only one part of an extraordinary period in everyone’s lives.

The discussion then turns to the present.

Has Newcastle’s squad improved as much as it should have since the takeover? Are there players from Bruce’s team who would strengthen today’s starting eleven? And how much patience should supporters have with the club’s latest recruits?

With the international break finally ending, there’s a round up of Newcastle players representing their countries before attention switches to Arsenal’s visit and the potentially awkward reception awaiting former Magpies favourite Bruno Guimarães.

Plenty of nostalgia, disagreement and the usual irreverent humour in another edition of The Mag Pod.

‘Silly season’ – or as it is better known, the ‘International break’, the two week hiatus in real West Ham-related football content to report, does occasionally throw up controversial, eyebrow raising or nonsensical articles which harassed authors have produced under the demands of editors or when faced by the blank page of content schedules. Bowen’s influence on games is unparalleled – whilst he may drift in or out of focus during a game, at any stage in the ninety minutes his contribution may be a goal, an assist or very often both. West Ham’s leading goal scorer in both the Premier League and the Championship is irreplaceable and vital to their hope of automatic promotion.

Now don’t get me wrong, Arne Engels is turning into a very useful midfield player and as he’s pushed further forward into an advanced role, should become more influential on games as befits his £22 million championship record-breaking transfer fee. #2045. Mavropanos departure claim produces a ‘meh’ response – and here’s why | West Ham News

Had the news filtered through in August, as West Ham prepared to do battle in the Championship, that Dinos Mavropanos had not signed the contract extension put in front of him after relegation, there might have been worry all around.

West Ham had just learned that Axel Disasi wasn’t coming back: The idea of Dinos leaving too would have been downright scary.

At least, going forward, Mavropanos was awesome. Five goals, from anyone, is not a bad return at all in just 15 out of 48 completed games. The lack of clean sheets, though, highlighted West Ham’s defensive vulnerabilities in which Mavropanos was, of course, a key component.

Reports first from Florian Plettenberg at Sky Germany, backed up more recently by KUMB, both claim that Mavropanos in fact did not sign the extension and that with a year and a half left on his West Ham contract, the club are open to selling him if the right offer comes along in January .

Great going forward but back to appearing a more shaky defender

‘Open to selling him’ is very different to ‘going to offload him’ and will presumably be dependent upon bringing a replacement into the club during the winter. West Ham have already parked Jean Clair Todibo in France for a season and so are short of one front line centre back.

Selling Dinos without a replacement isn’t going to be an option. However the willingness of the club to sell if the price is right shows common sense from a financial point of view and, let’s face it, Mavropanos has been no colossus defensively.

In any case there are any number of decent replacements available: Better to grab a solid transfer fee now than lose him for free in a year.

It is a reflection of his more modest defensive performances since Axel Disasi departed that news of his ‘possible’ departure creates little more than a shrug of the shoulders: In fact the back line has been poor for three or four years so this could be the start of something better.

#2043. Iraola will be beaming: Liverpool handed massive double injury boost ahead of Man United clash

Liverpool have been handed a significant double injury boost in the days leading up to their Premier League clash against Manchester United.

Andoni Iraola will be pleased that his players who were on international duty all seem set to return to Merseyside unscathed, even though Dominik Szoboszlai controversially played through the pain barrier for Hungary.

The Reds’ head coach is still waiting for a handful of long-term injury absentees to become available once more, but two of those have now taken a major step in their respective recoveries.

As reported by Paul Joyce for The Times, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni have returned to Liverpool first-team training, with both defenders having been sidelined for a number of months with serious knee injuries.

The Northern Ireland right-back has been out of action since January after he was struck down towards the end of the 0-0 draw at Arsenal; while the Italian teenager has been absent for even longer, not playing since rupturing his ACL on his Reds debut in September 2025.

The latter had been due to resume full training in early October before that staging post was delayed as medical staff took a cautious approach, but he’s now in the final stages of his recovery to full fitness and could resume playing in the coming weeks.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

While we wouldn’t bank on either of the Liverpool duo returning to matchday action in the concluding weeks of 2026, their resumption of first-team training comes as a huge step towards their long-awaited comebacks.

Bradley would very likely have made the right-back position his own this season had he not been sidelined, but thankfully Ronald Araujo has excelled in that role since joining on loan from Barcelona in August.

As for Leoni, it was beyond cruel that he tore his ACL towards the end of what had been a terrific Reds debut against Southampton 14 months ago, but he’s still only 19 and should hopefully have a hugely successful career still ahead of him.

Even when both players are cleared for a return to action, it’ll take time for them to properly get back into a matchday rhythm, and Iraola will surely bed them in gently after missing so much football over the past few months.

However, having them back in a full training feels like a significant step forward, and when the time comes for them to resume playing, it’ll be a wonderful sight for everyone associated with Liverpool.

#2042. Pressure grows for change after Hermansen howler | West Ham News

Whether or not Scott Parker has yet made up his mind about replacing his goalkeeper ahead of Saturday’s resumption of the Championship battle, the highlights reel from last night’s international tie between Denmark and Norway will prove compelling watching for West Ham’s new manager.

Quite possibly, if Parker hasn’t yet decided on a switch, seeing the latest error from his number one ‘keeper may well the tip the scales towards change: Hermansen dwelling too long on the ball and being dispossessed by Martin Odegaard after attempting a step-over inside his own ‘box turned out to be the pivotal moment in the game after Denmark had raced into a two goal lead against their rivals.

Hermansen’s howler proved to be the catalyst for a Norway recovery, scoring three and winning both the game and qualification for the last eight of the UEFA Nations League at the expense of the Danes, finishing second in the group thanks to their superior head-to-head record.

All too familiar expression of Hermansen’s anguish: the Dane needs a period of ‘reflection’ away from the firing line.

An expensive error indeed and one which cannot have escaped the attention of the coaching staff at Rush Green.

#2041. Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

The visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU

Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq

Blackburn drew level through an unlikely source just nine minutes later as McLoughlin headed in his first-ever goal in English football in more than 150 games when he met Ryoya Morishita’s cross from the right at the near post.

The home side had chances to retake the lead before the break as Lopez curled a shot narrowly over the top from 20-yards while Kieran Trippier teed up Mateus Mane for a chance as the teenager found the top of the net from distance.

Blackburn turned the game on its head minutes after the break as Gudjohnsen turned home Afolayan’s deflected ball in from the right from close range to stun Molineux into silence.

"It's brilliantly worked by Blackburn Rovers!" 💥Andri Guðjohnsen finishes from close range to turn the game around and the visitors the lead 👏 pic.twitter.com/vkKQQezicK

Peixoto introduced Jimenez from the bench on the hour mark but even the Mexican could not lift Wolves with Blackburn comfortable for long periods as frustration grew in the stands.

However, Alebiosu handled Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross from the left in injury time and the referee awarded a spot kick which allowed Jimenez to mark his Wolves return with an equaliser from 12-yards as he sent Balazs Toth the wrong way.

“I think it is a really harsh one. He [the referee] has to be sure at such a critical time of the game. And I do not think he can be sure. I think he has almost had a guess that he is in the box. It is such a big call.”

“We see the ref’s position. The fact the ref makes the decision to give the penalty in my opinion, it is a bigger decision to give it then to not. We have got the luxury of the replays and we are still not sure. His whole body is outside the box.”

“It looks outside the box to me [the penalty incident]. The still picture suggests to me it was outside the box. We can get better and we will have to. We have to be more dominant with the ball at times and be better in attack. We have done a lot of work on that in pre-season. Having been in this league a long time, the power of the dressing room is crucial and any motivation tool you can you use is important. I think we will be fine. You have to enjoy football and love it. I think the boys enjoyed it tonight.”

“Obviously frustrated. The boys did everything to get the three points but it is gutting in the end. I thought I was outside the box when the ball came in and the decision went against us. They are saying it is in the box and it is frustrating. We dug deep and thought we had it. I cannot fault everyone as we all put in a shift, it was just the final details with the penalty decision. We deserved the three points. If we play like that every week, we will go far in the table.”

Raul Jimenez reacts after his late penalty saved a point for Wolves against Blackburn 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/aXvVeWw6fc

“Before the game we were predicting Wolves would be right up there [this season] and we thought it would be a comfortable win. But that was not the case.  Blackburn gave a really good account of themselves and had lots of openings. [Cesar] Peixoto will be breathing a massive sigh of relief with that handball.”

“Wolves got away with one if I am being really honest. In terms of their second-half performance, they did not do anywhere near enough. I thought Blackburn were excellent throughout and deservedly took the lead. It is a huge decision [to give the penalty], but in the end Raul Jimenez steps up to get his side the point. [Cesar Peixoto] will be delighted to get something in the end.”

Bentley spills the corner but gets a free-kick. Moments later, the referee blows his whistle for the final time and the game ends level at 2-2. A dramatic opening night of the new Championship season at Molineux. If the Championship continues in this vein all season, it will be one hell of a year.

Blackburn nearly score a late winner as Garrett’s shot is tipped over the bar by Bentley for a later Blackburn corner.

He sends Toth the wrong way and calmly slots home to bring Wolves level in added time. That penalty decision will certainly create some debate. The Championship is always full of drama and we get some on opening night.

LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU

It just had to be. Jimenez rescues Wolves from the penalty spot.

Drama on the opening night of the campaign.

Relief for Wolves, heartbreak for Blackburn.

Late drama at Molineux! The cross is sent in from the left and the ball strikes the arm Alebiosu on the edge of the box. Was it inside or outside the penalty area? It is definitely handball but was it outside the box? It was very, very close but there is no VAR in the Championship so the penalty will stand.

Four added minutes. Are we on the verge of seeing the first shock of the new Championship season on opening night?

Four minutes added. Not even a reaction from the home crowd.

Wolves are desperately running out of time and Blackburn still look comfortable.

Home fans are beginning to filter out slowly.

Mosquera is still struggling but he has come back on whilst limping around. I cannot imagine there will be too much in terms of added time, either three or four minutes would be my guess, no more.

Ohashi is played in behind and goes down under a challenge from Toti on the edge of the Wolves box but those appeals are waved away.

Mosquera has gone down again and he may not be able to continue as he receives treatment on the sidelines. Wolves may be ending this game down to 10 men.

Fevrier’s shot from outside the Wolves penalty area is blocked and spins behind for a corner in front of the travelling Blackburn fans. The corner comes to nothing.

Wolves struggling to create anything of note even with Jimenez’s introduction.

Centre-back Mosquera has gone up front but appears to be struggling with an injury. He’s jogged back to his natural position now.

Desperate long balls being sent forward but Blackburn look comfortable for now. The home fans are quite audibly unhappy with this second-half showing.

Wolves do not currently look like scoring an equaliser.

Mosquera is struggling with a knock but Wolves made all five changes. If he is unable to continue, Wolves will have to finish off with ten men.

The frustration inside Molineux is growing and the home fans want to see some more urgency from their side as they trail with under 10 minutes left.

Blackburn are now going to make their final two alterations of the night as Ribeiro and Garrett come on.

Wolves are going to make their final two substitutions as Lima and Chirewa replace Moller Wolfe and Andre.

Blackburn are looking pretty comfortable right now defending their lead and counter-attacking effectively.

Wolves want a penalty as Armstrong goes down inside the box after making a run in behind but the appeals are waved away. Rightly so as Armstrong was not fouled.

Wolves are pushing to find an equaliser but are struggling to carve out many genuine opportunities.

Ohashi is penalised for a foul on F Lopez not far outside the Blackburn penalty area and that was pretty harsh on Ohashi. Jimenez is lining this one up as is F Lopez.

The former takes but his effort hits the wall.

Wolves’ frustration right now is summed up by a dreadful cross from F Lopez from the right side of the box that goes behind for a goal kick. The TV cameras then turn to some of the Wolves fans, who look rather forlorn in the stands.

Double changes for both sides. For Wolves, Doyle and Tchatchoua come on. For Blackburn, Fevrier and Ohasi enter the fray.

You’d have thought a goal had gone in such is the reaction from the home crowd to Jimenez’s introduction. I have to say, I’m surprised Mane has made way but Jimenez will play through the middle with Armstrong moved out to the left.

Blackburn made a change earlier in the half with Wolverhampton-born Sam Morsy on for his Rovers debut. One manager going for it as the other attempts to shore things up.

Wolves’ last shot on target was all the way back in the 18th minute, when Munetsi put them in front. That is in fact their only shot on target tonight, compared to Blackburn’s four.

Should Wolves have been given a penalty? Jimenez goes down after Atcheson did stick out his leg but was there enough in it to give a penalty?

Jimenez is indeed now going to come on and Molineux rises to welcome him onto the pitch. The Jimenez scarfs go up around the ground and his song is sung. Mane goes off.

Munetsi, the scorer of Wolves’ goal, has a shot deflected from the edge of the box and it goes behind for a corner. Gudjohnsen, the scorer of Blackburn’s second, heads away at the front post.

Blackburn are the first to turn to their bench as one experienced midfielder replaces another with Morsy coming on for Forshaw.

Can Wolves turn the game back in their favour? It’s all a bit slow now from the hosts followed by the first signs of disgruntlement from the home supporters.

Molineux is stunned as the underdogs take the lead inside the opening five minutes of the second half. Tony Mowbray’s side have started well since the break and are rewarded. Forshaw is the third Blackburn player into the book tonight as the referee goes back to penalise the midfielder for an earlier foul on Andre. That was not Forshaw’s first foul either.

Mane wins it back for his side on the edge of his own penalty area and drives forward. He takes it across the halfway line before feeding a lovely pass to his right to find Armstrong, whose shot is blocked.

Mane comes close to a stunner. Trippier rolls the ball across the face of the penalty area to 18-year-old Mane, who takes on the shot first time but his effort goes just over the bar.

Wolves come close to restoring their lead. Mane drives inside from the left and plays the ball forward to F Lopez, who takes one touch before getting his shot away from just outside the box. He tries to pick out the top corner but it just misses the target.

Like London buses, two yellow cards come at once and another Blackburn player is into the book. It is their captain Cantwell who receives a yellow card for delaying the restart. Cantwell was not too impressed with that decision.

Both teams off the mark for the season now, a brilliant near-post run and header from McLoughlin who scores his first-ever goal in English football to level the game up.

Molineux briefly stunned into silence. A slight delay from the fans celebrating the header as well.

A cool finish from the midfielder after a bit of a drab start from the home side.

Wolves fans make their feelings about VAR known following the goal. No VAR in the Championship of course but no VAR was needed for that anyway. A perfectly good goal.

Mane cuts inside from the left onto his preferred right foot and curls a dangerous ball into the box that is punched away by Toth in the Blackburn goal. 18-year-old Mane was one of very few bright spots for Wolves last season and in many ways it is a surprise that no Premier League teams have lured him back to the top flight quite yet. That could though still happen before the deadline.

The first goal of the Championship season comes against the run of play. It is a clinical, ruthless goal that comes from an incisive pass and clinical finish. Blackburn have definitely been the better side in these early exchanges, dominating possession and looking a threat going forward.

Blackburn may be heavy underdogs tonight but they have settled down well away at one of the favourites to get promoted. Tony Mowbray may well be seeing this as a good time to play Wolves away.

Alebiosu shows quick feet down Blackburn’s right and clips a cross to the back post, where Afolayan meets it but his header is just off target.

By contrast, Kieran Trippier’s first touch of the season is greeted by loud boos by the travelling Blackburn supporters.

When Wolverhampton Wanderers last attacked the Championship under a Portuguese manager new to English football, it proved a vintage season.

Molineux was under the spell of Nuno Espírito Santo in that 2017-18 campaign, and the big question is whether César Peixoto can lead a repeat nearly a decade later.

Peixoto was a surprise appointment in June, replacing Rob Edwards, and he has been entrusted with the mission of returning Wolves to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

“I have changed some things with set-pieces and some things in other moments of the game because I want the team to be organised and understand all the different moments within a match. During pre-season we have scored some goals from high pressing, but we will not be able to press high in every moment of every game. The players have to understand the game and recognise what each moment requires. It is important that we work as a team. When we can press high, we’ll press high. When we need to defend in a mid-block, we will stay organised. When the opposition pushes us deeper, which will sometimes happen, we have to be organised there as well.

“There are a lot of crosses in the Championship, for example, so the team needs to understand what to do in those situations. We want to play our football, be offensive and react strongly when we lose the ball, but we also need to understand the different moments of the game. I think we are at a good level to attack the Championship.”

Our experts have been having their say ahead of the new Championship season. A number of them believe Wolves will be promoted, including John Percy:

It is difficult to look beyond West Ham. Nuno Espírito Santo romped to the Championship title with Wolves in 2018 and remains a shrewd operator (along with his No 2 Rui Pedro Silva), while convincing Jarrod Bowen to stay is significant. I am going to go for Wolves and Middlesbrough as the other two promoted clubs.

The 2026/27 Championship season kicks off at Molineux as Wolves host Blackburn, with the home side hoping to put the bad memories of last season firmly behind them. There are new playoff rules in place for this season, with six places now up for grabs in the play-offs.

Wolves are aiming to return to the Premier League at the first attempt, having endured a miserable season in the top flight last year as they finished bottom with just three wins to their name. It has been a summer of change at the club as they chose to change managers. Rob Edwards lost his job in what was a shock move and was replaced by 46-year-old Cesar Peixoto, with this being his first head coaching position outside of his home country Portugal. Back in 2017/18, Wolves won the Championship title led by Peixoto’s compatriot Nuno Espirito Santo.

“I am ready,” Peixoto told Wolves’ club website. “We have worked very hard during pre-season, and I think we have had a great pre-season. All the players have worked very, very hard and they understand what I want from them. I am ready and confident going into the first game. Football is football, whether it is in Portugal or England, but there are different characteristics to the game here. We have watched, observed and analysed the Championship. We did that work before I came to the club, so we know what to expect.

“It is going to be a tough season with good teams, but we are prepared to fight for the three points game after game and week after week. We know what we want from the team and we know what our big goal is. We’re going to work very hard and fight to achieve that goal.”

They have brought in vast experience on the player side in the shape of Kieran Trippier and Raul Jimenez, who is back at Molineux three years after leaving for Fulham. Although they have lost Brazilian midfielder Joao Gomes to Aston Villa, most of their squad has stayed intact as they pursue promotion back to the top flight. It is a special year for the club as they celebrate their 150th anniversary.

Blackburn, led by experienced manager Tony Mowbray, did not enjoy a great season in the Championship last year, finishing down in 20th place and just five points above the relegation zone. 14 years have now passed since Blackburn last played in the top flight.

“I think it is a tough start,” Mowbray said. “On paper, I would suggest the first couple of games, particularly, jumped out as a tough start. One of the Premier League sides from last season, away from home. They have got a very talented squad, a pretty expensive squad. They have got some very good individual talent. Yet, there is an argument to say they have not won many football matches in the last calendar year. So, what we get, we will have to wait and see.”

These sides last met in the FA Cup during the 2024/25 season, with Wolves winning that fourth-round tie 2-0 thanks to goals from Matheus Cunha and Gomes, both of whom are now plying their trade elsewhere. The omens would appear to be on Wolves’ side as they are unbeaten in their last eight league meetings with Blackburn. Both sides progressed to the second round of the League Cup last weekend, with Wolves beating Port Vale 3-0 and Blackburn overcoming Burton Albion 2-1.

#2040. West Ham Receive Double Boost Following Kanté’s Mali Success

West Ham United midfielder Mohamadou Kanté has helped Mali qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations following a 2-0 victory over Rwanda on Tuesday evening. It’s another significant milestone for the young Hammer, who has only just made his senior international debut, and the good news doesn’t end there.

Mali secured qualification with two matches to spare, thanks to goals from Modibo Sagnan and Gaoussou Diarra in Kigali. Kanté came off the bench in the 64th minute, having made his international debut in Friday’s 3-2 victory over the same opponents.

Mali are now guaranteed a place at next summer’s finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. And having discovered precisely when the tournament will take place, I have to say I’m absolutely delighted for Kanté. In fact, it’s double delight as far as I’m concerned.

First and foremost, massive congratulations to Kanté.

Having decided to switch his international allegiance from France to Mali, he’s already playing senior international football and now has a major tournament to look forward to.

It’s a tremendous achievement, particularly when you consider how quickly things have happened for him this season.

Kanté has been one of West Ham’s most impressive players, and his international recognition is thoroughly deserved.

As Claret & Hugh recently reported following his international debut, his performances for the Hammers have now been rewarded with an opportunity to establish himself on the international stage.

But there’s another reason I’m so pleased about this news, and it’s one that makes a massive difference from a West Ham perspective.

I’ve always disliked the fact that the Africa Cup of Nations has so often been plonked directly in the middle of the domestic football season.

As we saw during the last campaign, the losses of both our full-backs, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and El-Hadji Malick Diouf, had a massive impact on West Ham.

Hammers youngster Mohamadou Kanté will be playing in the AFCON

Indeed, I wrote about the problem before their departure for AFCON, when we were facing the prospect of losing two important defenders at a particularly difficult time.

It was hugely frustrating, and I’ve never particularly liked the idea of clubs losing key players for several weeks in the middle of their league campaigns.

But this time, thank goodness, it’s different.

The Confederation of African Football has confirmed that the 2027 tournament will take place from 19 June to 17 July, rather than during the winter months.

That means Kanté can enjoy the experience of representing Mali at a major international tournament without West Ham having to lose him in the middle of the Championship season.

Of course, there’s still the question of whether Kanté will even be at West Ham next summer. Who’s to say he’ll still be at the club next year?

But assuming he is, the timing means Scott Parker won’t suddenly have to manage without one of his most important midfielders for several weeks during a promotion campaign.

#2039. West Ham’s £18m Castellanos Problem Could Prove Difficult To Solve

Reports originating from Argentine journalist Renzo Pantich have suggested that Taty Castellanos wants to leave West Ham United and has already rejected a lucrative offer from Flamengo in favour of remaining in Europe.

Where in Europe, one may ask – and that’s a question no one knows!

Pantich’s claim has generated plenty of attention, but when you dig beneath the surface, it raises a lot of questions!

The suggestion appears to be that by rejecting Flamengo, Castellanos has demonstrated a desire to leave West Ham while remaining in Europe. Yet that conclusion ignores several important realities.

Firstly, Flamengo are reportedly facing financial difficulties with high transfer debts and sponsorship issues due to the Brazilian government banning football clubs from receiving payments from betting and online casinos.

The Brazilian midfielder reportedly accepted a sizeable wage reduction to join Flamengo. It seems highly unlikely that Castellanos, who is approaching what should be the peak years of his career, would be prepared to make a similar sacrifice.

Flamengo’s interest in the striker is nothing new. The Rio giants admired him during his time at Lazio but were unable to make a deal happen because the finances simply didn’t work. The transfer fee and salary package required were beyond what they were prepared to pay. Indeed, it was suggested at the time the player wanted to remain in Europe – sounds like a déjà vu moment!?

Taty wants to leave but who can realistically afford him?

Lastly, and most importantly, there is no mention of any transfer discussions between West Ham and Flamengo on any news wires.

Nobody doubts the emotional attraction. Castellanos has never hidden his admiration for the Argentine giants, and a move back home would undoubtedly appeal on a personal level. The problem is affordability.

Matching a transfer fee acceptable to West Ham while also covering the striker’s wages would represent a huge financial commitment, even for one of South America’s biggest clubs. As C&H has previously reported, River Plate simply can’t afford the player.

In fact, C&H exclusively revealed that it is West Ham who have been actively exploring ways of finding a buyer for the underperforming forward rather than the player agitating for a move.

Despite accepting a wage reduction following West Ham’s relegation, Castellanos remains on a highly attractive contract. His current deal runs until 2030 and includes a one-year club option.

Even following the Championship wage reduction, he is still earning only marginally less than the reported £48,000 per week he received at Lazio.

Should West Ham return to the Premier League this season and want to activate that extension, Castellanos could still have effectively four years of Premier League-level earnings ahead of him.

At around £77,000 per week, that’s potentially close to £18 million in future wages.

Those are numbers very few clubs outside England’s top flight can realistically match.

There will almost certainly need to be compromise from both sides. West Ham appear keen to move the striker on, while Castellanos may have to accept that replacing those wages elsewhere will be extremely difficult.

For all the speculation, one thing seems clear: finding a buyer may prove considerably harder than finding rumours!

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2037. “Grim Reading” West Ham’s London Stadium Financial Problem Just Got Worse

West Ham supporters hoping that relegation to the Championship might bring some financial relief to the London Stadium’s troubled finances may be in for a shock.

The latest accounts for London Stadium LLP, covering the year ending March 2026, reveal an operation still struggling financially, with annual losses of £20.6m, negative net assets of almost £247m and a staggering £243.7m provision for expected losses under its long-term contractual arrangements.

While the figures represent an improvement on the previous year, the stadium remains heavily dependent on financial support from the Greater London Authority and, ultimately, London taxpayers.

But perhaps the most significant revelation for Hammers supporters is the financial impact of relegation.

The biggest concern in the accounts is an onerous contract provision of £243.7m.

In simple terms, this represents the stadium operator’s estimate of future losses from its long-term contractual commitments, principally its concession agreement with West Ham and its access agreement with UK Athletics.

The provision has increased from £206.7m in March 2024 to £241.5m in March 2025 and now £243.7m.

It is not a bill that needs paying immediately, but it highlights the scale of the financial challenge facing the stadium.

The London Stadium financial figures make for grim reading

The accounts explicitly acknowledge the financial consequences of West Ham dropping out of the Premier League.

The stadium’s financial forecasts currently assume the Hammers will return to the top flight after just one season in the Championship.

Should West Ham remain outside the Premier League for another season, the estimated contractual loss provision would increase by a further £2.3m.

That is a sobering admission and demonstrates just how important Premier League football is to the stadium’s financial model.

London Stadium generated revenue of £13.6m during the year, including £4.8m received from West Ham for its use of the ground.

However, this is nowhere near enough to make the operation financially sustainable.

The accounts confirm that the stadium continues to rely on Greater London Authority funding, with a capital contribution of £21.876m received during the year.

The GLA has also provided a letter of support covering at least 12 months from approval of the accounts.

In other words, despite being home to a Premier League football club for almost a decade, the stadium remains dependent on public-sector financial backing.

There was also an interesting development in the long-running financial dispute between West Ham and London Stadium LLP.

The disagreement concerned a payment of approximately £3.6m, plus interest, connected with Daniel Křetínský’s investment in West Ham.

Following a legal battle and an appeal, London Stadium ultimately won the case, with the money released from escrow in April 2026.

The accounts reversed a £3.941m provision previously made for the dispute, helping improve the reported financial result.

There are clearly significant challenges ahead.

The stadium’s financial future depends on West Ham returning to the Premier League, attracting new commercial partnerships, maintaining GLA support and managing its expensive long-term contractual commitments.

The recent departure of chief executive Graham Gilmore after nine years in the role adds another layer of uncertainty, with operations director Darren Raczkowski stepping in as interim chief executive.

For West Ham supporters, there is an uncomfortable irony.

The club’s move to the London Stadium was supposed to provide a modern home and a platform for growth, while delivering a lasting legacy for London.

Yet almost a decade later, the stadium is still losing millions, carries an enormous long-term contractual burden and remains reliant on public money.

And with West Ham now in the Championship, the financial assumptions underpinning the stadium’s future are already under greater pressure.

The big question is how much longer London taxpayers will be expected to support an operation that has yet to demonstrate it can stand on its own two feet.

#2036. West Ham Boss Parker Makes January Admission On talkSPORT

West Ham United manager Scott Parker has made it clear that January transfers are not currently at the forefront of his thinking, despite the Hammers’ obvious need to strengthen their squad. Speaking to talkSPORT this morning, Parker suggested that his immediate priority is working with the players already at his disposal.

Asked directly whether West Ham would have money to spend and bring in fresh faces, Parker acknowledged that the January window would be considered if necessary. However, he explained that since arriving at Rush Green, his attention has been almost entirely focused on his players and coaching staff.

Personally, I think he’s absolutely right. Even with the best will in the world, and assuming West Ham bring in some brilliant players in January, there are still nearly two months’ worth of results to fight for with the players currently available. Parker would be absolutely mad to spend too much time concentrating on transfers now.

Speaking during his talkSPORT interview, Parker explained that he had barely spoken to anybody outside his immediate coaching environment since taking charge.

“I’m sure there’ll be an eye in January if need be,” he said, before explaining that his main priority was establishing the habits and principles he wants from his players.

West Ham have a director of football in Nils Koppen, who can deal with precisely this type of thing. There is no reason for Parker to be spending his first few weeks in the job obsessing about transfer targets when the current squad desperately needs coaching.

After all, Claret & Hugh has already revealed that Koppen is working on January recruitment, including an approach to a potential striker signing.

The work is happening behind the scenes, and Parker doesn’t need to be personally involved in every conversation.

Parker can outsource his transfer concerns to Koppen

As Claret & Hugh has already revealed following contact with the football club, January business is being planned.

Every message we’ve received from sources inside the club indicates that promotion back to the Premier League is the overwhelming priority.

Of course, I expect funds to be made available in January. That doesn’t mean West Ham have unlimited money to spend, but the club’s determination to get promoted has been made abundantly clear.

And whilst we’ve previously reported on the financial constraints surrounding January recruitment, that doesn’t mean the club will simply sit on its hands.

But the January transfer window cannot rescue the points we fail to collect in November and December.

That is why Parker is right to concentrate on coaching.

Another interesting aspect of the interview was Parker’s discussion of the mentality required to succeed in the Championship.

He explained that players coming down from the Premier League have often spent months losing football matches, only to find themselves suddenly expected to win almost every week.

That psychological transition, he suggested, can be enormous.

The players clearly have ability, but Parker needs to establish the mentality and habits that allow them to produce it consistently.

If he can do that over the next few weeks, West Ham will be in a considerably stronger position when January arrives.

And if Koppen can then strengthen the areas that need improving, all the better.

For now, though, I’m delighted Parker is concentrating on the job immediately in front of him.

#2035. Premier League KMI Panel unanimously admits to another refereeing error which wronged Liverpool

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has adjudged that Liverpool had a penalty wrongly given against them in a recent fixture.

The Reds won their last game before the international break, beating Crystal Palace 3-1 at Selhurst Park, although Alisson Becker was denied a clean sheet by a stoppage-time spot kick awarded to the home side and converted by Eddie Nketiah.

The penalty was awarded for what referee Tony Harrington deemed to be a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio when the two players unfortunately clashed heads, and Andoni Iraola said afterwards that he was ‘very upset‘ over that decision.

The Premier League’s KMI Panel has now published its findings from the most recent top-flight matchday (via premierleague.com), and all five independent assessors adjudged that the penalty award against Liverpool was incorrect.

However, there was also unanimous agreement that VAR was right not to intervene, as it was decreed that no ‘clear and obvious’ error had taken place.

The panel concluded: ‘The panel unanimously felt that the referee’s call of a penalty for a challenge by Kerkez on Osorio was incorrect, with the contact being inevitable given the jumping actions of both players.

‘However, the non-intervention of VAR was supported on the basis it was not a clear and obvious error.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Liverpool fans must be getting sick of hearing from the Premier League’s KMI Panel at this stage, with this incident coming fresh off the back of the panel ruling that we should’ve had a penalty for Jurrien Timber’s blatant shirt pull on Alexander Isak in the 0-1 defeat to Arsenal.

The incident with Kerkez and Osorio wasn’t as black-and-white, but the decision to award a spot kick still felt rather curious at the time. Luckily for Harrington, it came too late to have any major bearing on the overall result at Selhurst Park.

Still, to hear that an independent panel unanimously acknowledged that the Reds were wronged by another refereeing error is galling for everyone associated with LFC, and yet again it calls into question the standads of officiating in the Premier League.

It’s the kind of inconsistency between Kerkez having a spot kick given against him for a 50/50 duel, and Timber getting away with a blatant infringement, which drives players, coaches, fans and pundits absolutely berserk.

Thankfully the decision in the Palace game didn’t do any lasting harm for Liverpool, but you get the sense that it won’t be long before another contentious decision goes against us and the KPI Panel is wheeled out to tell us what we can already deduce for ourselves.

West Ham United have reportedly joined Birmingham City and Southampton in monitoring Malmö FF midfielder Jovan Milosavljević, with the 19-year-old Serbian attracting attention ahead of the January transfer window.
